sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 (primary PDF): Management of Care 10-16% of items, including 'Prioritize the delivery of client care based on acuity' and 'Provide and receive handoff of care (report) on assigned clients'; Reduction of Risk Potential includes 'Recognize trends and changes in client condition and intervene as needed'. The test plan does not name SBAR or rapid response teams.

The objective and its secondary objectives are the course's own titles, built from the 2026 test plan. Delegation wording (the nurse cannot delegate assessment, evaluation or the care of unstable clients; assignment to another RN is a handoff) is the course's own, from the NCSBN/ANA delegation guidelines it cites; not re-fetched for this scenario.

brief.situation: 07:30 on a surgical unit. You are the RN for four clients, with one nursing assistant; the charge nurse has no assignment this morning. Night shift's report is done.
handover: Bed 10, Ms. Ortiz, 45, day 1 after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy: asked for her oral pain medicine at 07:25, pain 6/10, last dose 03:00. Stable.
Bed 11, Mr. Kim, 70, for discharge at 09:30 after a hernia repair: needs his discharge teaching. Stable.
Bed 12, Mr. Davis, 68, day 2 after a bowel resection: at 06:00 the assistant charted HR 104, RR 22, temperature 38.1, BP 112/70. Night shift says he was 'a bit restless'.
Bed 14, Mrs. Patel, 59, type 2 diabetes: rapid-acting insulin is due with breakfast at 08:00. Stable.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Tasks you do yourself take time and you can do one at a time; the tile marked You shows what you are on. The nursing assistant and the charge nurse can take tasks within their roles.
Bed 12's vital signs show only when someone measures them.
Partway through you are asked to write how you are ranking your clients. The case ends at 09:30, then a debrief scores what you did.

rank.question: Rank your four clients for the next hour and say why. What do you do about Bed 12 right now?

parts.label: Ranking
parts.criteria: Puts Bed 12 first because his cues (rising HR and RR, fever, falling BP, new confusion, a tender distended abdomen after bowel surgery) say unstable and worsening, ahead of a stable client's pain request, a due insulin and teaching; notes that who asked first does not set the order.
parts.modelAnswer: Bed 12 first: his 06:00 vital signs were already off and now he is more tachycardic, tachypneic, febrile, hypotensive and confused after bowel surgery. That is an unstable client. Bed 14's insulin is time-bound with the tray, Bed 10's pain is real but she is stable, and Bed 11's teaching can be handed to the charge nurse.

parts.label: Bed 12 now
parts.criteria: Escalates at once with an SBAR that names sepsis and asks the provider to come (or activates the rapid response team, and uses the chain of command if the answer is to wait); carries out cultures before the antibiotic without delaying it; keeps the assessment of an unstable client with the RN and delegates only tasks within the assistant's role.
parts.modelAnswer: Call the surgical resident with an SBAR naming sepsis and asking them to come now, or call the rapid response team since he meets the criteria; if told to recheck in an hour, go up the chain. Draw cultures and a lactate, then start the fluid and antibiotic. Keep his assessment myself; ask the assistant for Bed 14's tray set-up and the charge nurse for Bed 11's teaching.

collapse.headline: Bed 12 collapsed
collapse.body: His 06:00 vital signs were already a warning. Find when you first saw him, when someone who could treat him arrived, and what you did first instead.

rescued.headline: Bed 12 rescued early
rescued.body: Acuity, not the order of requests, set your priorities; you escalated in minutes and kept the assessment yourself. Check the other three clients: the expert path also hands stable tasks to the assistant and the charge nurse so nobody else waits.

rescuedLate.headline: Treated, by a slower route
rescuedLate.body: He is being treated, but check what you did first, how long the escalation took, whether a 'recheck in an hour' was accepted, and who assessed him.

time_up.headline: Bed 12 never treated
time_up.body: Two hours went to stable clients while the unstable one worsened. Rank by acuity and escalate up the chain when the first answer is to wait.

scoring.modelReasoning: Prioritize by acuity, not by who asked first. Bed 12 is a post-operative client with abnormal vital signs at 06:00 that are now worse, new confusion and a tender, distended abdomen: an unstable client with probable sepsis (an anastomotic leak is the worry). See him first, then escalate at once with an SBAR that names the concern and asks for what he needs, or activate the rapid response team when he meets the criteria; if the answer is to wait and the concern stands, go up the chain of command. Draw cultures before the antibiotic without delaying it, and start the fluid and antibiotic promptly. Assessment of an unstable client cannot be delegated; give the assistant tasks within the role and hand stable RN tasks (teaching, a due insulin) to another RN.

notDelegable.ask: While you assess: which of these could you hand to the nursing assistant right now?

choices.label: Setting up Bed 14's tray and morning care

notDelegable.explain: Morning care and tray set-up are within the assistant's role. Judging whether an unstable client is okay is assessment, and teaching is the nurse's: neither is delegated to assistive personnel. Teaching can go to another RN.

cultures.ask: Why draw the cultures before the antibiotic, and what if they would take an hour?

choices.label: Before, unless it would delay the antibiotic
Always before, however long it takes

cultures.explain: Cultures first so the antibiotic does not hide the organism, but not at the cost of a delay: the antibiotic is time-critical in possible septic shock.
